title: Request Provenance & Decision Trace Patterns
author: Lena Park
content:
Overview:
This document defines our patterns and operational guidance for request provenance and decision trace capture in the serving runtime. The goal is a compact, actionable trace that records the sequence of deterministic and policy-driven decisions made for each request (routing, kernel selection, quantization path, cache behavior, priority/crediting), and ties those decisions to profiling events and benchmark artifacts for fast triage.

Why we need this:
- Reduce time-to-blame for performance regressions and correctness incidents by exposing causal decisions.
- Enable reproducible investigations: the same request + recorded decisions should allow offline replay/tests.
- Provide inputs to cost accounting, model rollout analysis, and automated fallback validation.

Design goals:
- Minimal runtime overhead: target median added latency <= 0.5% and p99 < 1.0% for traced requests.
- Deterministic schema with optional enrichment fields to allow incremental rollouts.
- Sample-aware: full traces for 0.1% of requests by default, dynamic sampling for incidents or experiments.
- Privacy-conscious: do not record raw user inputs; record hashes/prefixes and model identifiers.

Trace model (canonical fields):
- trace_id: unique 128-bit hex string
- request_id: the per-request correlation id seen by the control plane
- sample_rate: sampling multiplier when trace was captured (e.g. 0.001)
- timestamp: ISO-8601 receive time
- origin: source type (api, dedicated, private)
- route: API route name or model route id
- tenant: tenant id (internal opaque id)
- user_data_hash: sha256 prefix (first 8 hex chars) of request content OR "masked" when not available
- seq_length: requested max tokens / prompt length bucket
- decisions: ordered list of decision events (see example below)
- kernel_profile_ref: short id linking to the kernel profiling snapshot (if available)
- kvcache_hits: number of KV cache prefix hits observed
- cost_estimate_units: token-equivalent units used for quick billing breakdown
- fallback_path: list of fallbacks invoked (empty if none)
- outcome: success | degraded | failed

Implementation note: the primary trace object must be a single JSON blob no larger than 4KB in production sampling; enrichment objects (large kernel profiles, microprofiles) are referenced by id and stored separately.

Decision event schema (textual table):
| field | description | examples |
|---|---|---|
| ordinal | integer ordering for causal sequence | 0,1,2 |
| ts | event ISO time relative to trace start | +3.2ms |
| actor | subsystem making decision | router, policy-engine, kernel-mapper, kvcache |
| decision | short token representing choice | route:region-us-east-1, kernel:fp16-q5 |
| reason | concise reason or rule id | capacity-constrained, latency-slo |
| metadata | small key=value pairs (flat) | core_count=1;quant_profile=q5 |

Instrumentation points (where to emit decision events):
1) Ingress routing: record top-k route candidates, selected route, and rule id.
2) Auth/tenant resolution: tenant id derivation and any policy overrides.
3) Model variant selection: model id, version, quantization profile, and compatibility hint.
4) Kernel mapper: chosen kernel binary id, block size, and shard topology.
5) Scheduling crediting: priority class, kernel credit debit snapshot.
6) KV cache layer: prefix lookup result, partial fill, eviction hint.
7) Batching window decisions: batch size, wait time, and cause (idle/burst).
8) Fallback decisions: model swap, region fallback, or feature flag disable.

Sampling and retention policy:
- Default sampling: 0.1% global for production requests.
- On-incident sampling: increase to 10% for affected routes via runtime flag.
- Experiment sampling: per-release experiment tags allow targeted 5% sampling for test cohorts.
- Retention: full trace records retained for 90 days; referenced kernel profiles retained for 365 days.
- Access controls: traces are internal-only; any trace access must be via RBACed consoles and audited.

Trace telemetry SLOs and overhead budget:
- Trace emission error rate: < 0.01% of traced requests may fail to persist.
- Max added latency (median): 0.5% of request median latency.
- CPU overhead: prefer async, batched persist writes; budget 0.2 vCPU per 1000 RPS of traced streams.
- Storage budget: estimate 3MB per 1k full traces per day (adjust by enrichment usage).

Correlating traces with profiling and benchmark artifacts:
1) Kernel profiling snapshot linkage: include kernel_profile_ref (short id) in trace that maps to a per-node microprofile (occupancy, register use, latency histogram).
2) Benchmark run mapping: records produced during A/B tests must include experiment_id and commit hash in trace metadata.
3) Offline replay input: traces flagged with reproducible=true must include sufficient bucketed inputs and model version to run the same code path in staging.

Operational runbook: triage using decision traces (short):
1) Reproduce the incident window: collect traces for the problem window (use on-incident sampling to increase capture).
2) Identify decision divergence: look for traces where decision sequences differ from baseline (kernel change, fallback trigger, scheduling policy).
3) Correlate with kernel_profile_ref and node telemetry (GPU temp, stall counters).
4) If kernel choice changed unexpectedly, run targeted microbenchmark using the same kernel_profile_ref and seq_length bucket.
5) Mitigation options (ordered by safety): roll back kernel mapping change, temporary increased sampling + capture full profiles, enable fallback to previous variant, scale dedicated pool.
6) Post-incident: attach relevant traces to incident page, rerun small replay suite to validate regression fix.

Incident-specific procedures (detailed):
- High tail latency on hosted API:
  1) Increase tracing to 5% for the affected route for 15 minutes.
  2) Run an automated trace-diff: group by (kernel binary id, batch size, seq_length).
  3) If group with higher p99 has a common kernel id, escalate to kernel-owner.
- Unexpected fallback storms:
  1) Query traces with fallback_path length > 0 and group by reason.
  2) If reason is capacity-constrained, consult capacity-dashboard and consider temporary autoscale bump.

Best practices for developers and SREs:
- Prefer referencing trace ids in PRs that touch kernel selection or routing logic.
- When adding a new decision point, add a single event and avoid verbose metadata; use a separate enrichment store for large objects.
- Use hashing and bucketing for any user content stored in traces to preserve privacy.

Implementation checklist (minimal viable trace support):
- [ ] Add trace emission hook at ingress with trace_id and request context.
- [ ] Add decision event writer library (lightweight, flat map API).
- [ ] Implement async tracer to persist to internal trace store with batching.
- [ ] Add kernel_profile_ref generation and store microprofiles separately.
- [ ] Add runtime flags for sampling multipliers per route.
- [ ] Add console query that links from request_id -> trace_id -> kernel_profile_ref.

Appendix B — Frequently asked questions:
Q: Will traces include prompt text?
A: No. We record hashed prefixes and bucketed lengths only to avoid sensitive data in traces. If a tenant requests full content capture for a private deployment, that must be enabled under a restricted policy and stored in an encrypted enrichment store.

Q: How do we avoid trace storming when an incident spike occurs?
A: Sampling multipliers are capped and require an ops-token to exceed 10% for a route. The tracing pipeline has a backpressure mechanism that drops the lowest-priority enrichment payloads first.
